paragraphs: Zetim vaanabim asur lischatan min hattora, ki zeh tolada dedash vechayyab min hattora; abal sechitat tutim verimmonim asur middibre soperim, vaapillu en lo tzorek bemashqeh; mihu muttar lischot kol ellu, apillu zetim vaanabim, letok haokel, demashqeh habba letok haokel hu keokel dame, vahare zeh kemaprid okel meokel; mihu, eno muttar ella davqa letok haokel, abal letok mayim o shear mashqeh, asur.

clarification.explanation: Squeezing olives and grapes is Torah-forbidden, since it is considered a derivative of the labor of threshing. Squeezing mulberries and pomegranates is forbidden only rabbinically, even if one has no need at all for the liquid that emerges from them. However, it is permitted to squeeze all these fruits — even olives and grapes — directly into a cooked dish or food, since a liquid squeezed into food is considered like the food itself, and this is considered separating food from food rather than forbidden squeezing. But this leniency applies only when squeezing directly into food — if squeezing into water or another beverage, it is forbidden.
takeaways: Squeezing olives and grapes is Torah-forbidden, and squeezing mulberries and pomegranates is rabbinically forbidden.
It is permitted to squeeze all of these directly into food (not into a beverage), since a liquid entering food is considered like the food.

paragraphs: Mashqim shezzabu mealehen beshabbat mizzetim vaanabim, apillu shehem omedim laakila asurim ad laereb, gezera shemma yischot beyadayim; abal tutim verimmonim, im omedim laakila, mashqin hayyotzeim mehem muttarim; veim omedin lemashqin, az hammashqin hayyotzeim mealehen asurim.

clarification.explanation: Beverages that dripped on their own on the Sabbath from olives and grapes — even if the fruit itself is intended for eating — are forbidden to drink until the Sabbath's conclusion, out of concern that one might come to actually squeeze them by hand. By contrast, mulberries and pomegranates — if they are intended for eating, the beverage that drips from them on its own is permitted. But if the mulberries or pomegranates themselves are intended for a beverage (not for eating), then the beverage that drips from them on its own is forbidden.
takeaways: A beverage that drips on its own from olives and grapes on the Sabbath is always forbidden, out of concern one might come to actually squeeze them.
A beverage that drips on its own from mulberries and pomegranates depends on the fruit's intended use — if for eating, the beverage is permitted; if for a beverage, it is forbidden.

paragraphs: Shear perot chutz mizzetim vaanabim verimmonim hannizkarim leel, im sochatan baabur sheyyesh lo tzorek bammashqin shellahem, asur; abal im sochatan lerakkek o lematteq happeri, kegon perot viraqot hakkebushin beme-melach vekayyotze shessochatan kede lemateqam ulerukkekem, shari; ki kol sheeno tzarik ledabar hammitpareq dehaynu memehen, en bazeh mishshum dash umepareq. velaken asur lischot peri haadama shehu abbetichin hashshechorim sheqqorin bearbe "roqi" kede lishtot mayim shellahem; v"g deyesh mattirin beperot sheen derek bene-adam lischatan, usebira lehu daapillu im zeh mitkavven lischatan lishtot memehen, batela dato etzel kol adam veshari, mikkol maqom yesh lachush lisbarat haoserin, veen lischot shum peri im mitkavven lehotzi mashqeh lishtoto, mihu gam lisbarat haoserin, shari lischot perot ellu letok keli reqan im yirtzeh latet mashqeh shellahem letok haokel, o im yirtzeh letabbel bemashqeh maakol, vela baenan lischot letok haokel mammash ella raq zetim vaanabim vetutim verimmonim bilbad, yaan ki shear perot, meachar deen derek haolam lischatan leshem mashqeh, hakkol yodeim keshessochet otam hu sochatan letzorek hammaakol velo leshem mashqeh.

clarification.explanation: Other fruits (besides olives, grapes, and pomegranates mentioned above) — if squeezed in order to obtain the liquid inside them, this is forbidden. But if squeezed only to soften the fruit or sweeten it (like vegetables and fruits pickled in brine that are squeezed to soften and sweeten them), this is permitted — since the rule is that as long as a person does not intend to obtain the liquid itself, there is no prohibition of threshing or extracting. Therefore it is forbidden to squeeze the fruit called "raqi" (a type of black melon) in order to drink its juices. There are lenient opinions regarding fruits that people do not normally squeeze, holding that even if one intends to drink the beverage, his intent is void since this is not the normal way; but nevertheless one should be concerned for the stricter opinions and not squeeze any fruit with the intent of drinking its juices. Nevertheless, even according to the stricter opinions, it is permitted to squeeze these fruits into an empty vessel if the intent is to add the liquid to food, or to dip food in it — and only with olives, grapes, mulberries, and pomegranates must one squeeze directly into the food itself, since with other fruits, since people do not normally squeeze them for a beverage, it is clear to all that the intent is for food and not for a beverage.
takeaways: Squeezing a fruit to obtain the liquid itself is forbidden, but squeezing it only to soften or sweeten the fruit itself is permitted.
With fruits not normally squeezed for a beverage, it is permitted to squeeze even into an empty vessel, since the intent is clearly for food.

paragraphs: "p shemmuttar lischot kol mine perot vaapillu zetim vaanabim letok qedera sheyyesh bah okel, mikkol maqom habboser, yesh oserim lischatu apillu letok haokel, hoil veeno rauy laakila bipne atzmo, dedavqa eshkol shehu rauy laakila have lah kemaprid okel meokel veshare, abal boser sheeno rauy laakila, en zeh kemaprid okel meokel; vaapillu haokelo, batela dato etzel kol adam. vehu haddin lekol perot sheenam reuyim laakila deasur lischatan gam letok haokel. velaken peri chimmutz sheqqorin bearbi "dibdayeb" (peri etz baal qelippa aba umara shehi hanneekelet mimmennu), asur lischatu apillu letok haokel, mippene shezzeh eno rauy laakila, abal peri sheqqorin bearbe "nryng" (peri hadar chimmutz mar), rauy laakila hu, umuttar lischatu letok haokel. veken nohagin poh irenu y" lischot peri sheqqorin "nryng" betok habbetzim beshabbat; venireh deshare lischatu gam letok keli reqan kede lehannicha et hammashqeh beokel, o kede letabbel bemashqeh pat vekayyotze, abal asur lischatu letok keli reqan velishtoto kemo shehu.

clarification.explanation: Although it is permitted to squeeze all kinds of fruit, including olives and grapes, into a pot containing food, nevertheless with unripe grapes, some hold it is forbidden to squeeze them even into food, since they are not fit for eating on their own. The rule is that only a fruit fit for eating is considered, when squeezed into food, as "separating food from food" and therefore permitted; but unripe fruit, which is not fit for eating, is not considered so, and even one who nonetheless eats it — his intent is void. The same law applies to any fruit unfit for eating — it is forbidden to squeeze it even into food. Therefore the sour fruit called "dabdib" (with a thick, bitter peel that is the part eaten) is forbidden to squeeze even into food, since it is unfit for eating. By contrast, the citrus fruit called "narinj" (sour and bitter) is indeed fit for eating, and therefore it is permitted to squeeze it into food — and so the practice in Baghdad is to squeeze it into eggs on the Sabbath. It is also permitted to squeeze it into an empty vessel if the intent is to place the liquid on food or to dip bread in it, but it is forbidden to squeeze it into an empty vessel in order to drink it as is.
takeaways: Unripe grapes and fruits unfit for eating on their own — forbidden to squeeze even into food.
A sour citrus fruit (narinj) is fit for eating and therefore may be squeezed into food, but not into an empty vessel for drinking alone.

paragraphs: "limonim" chimmutz, yesh oserim lischatu letok keli reqan "p sherotzeh litteno letok haokel, mippene ki bimqomot sheyyesh mimmennu harbeh, darkam lischot harbeh mimmennu letzorek hammashqeh sheqqorin "lymvndh", umemallein mimmennu chabiyyot gedolot letzorek hannizkar. v"g demera"n za"l hittir lischatu - nirin dibre haoserim bazzeman hazzeh; velaken hiskimu haacharonim shello lischatu letok keli reqan, veken hiskim haggaon chida" za"l. umi sherotzeh laasot "lymvndh" shehu mashqeh hannischat min hallimonim hannizkar im sukkar umayim, yasim techilla hassoker bikli veyischat hallimonim hannizkar al hassoker atzmo shehu okel, veaach"k yannicha hammayim, abal lo yannicha hammayim qodem sechitat hallimonim hannizkar, venatenu siman al zeh: "vehinneh sullam mutztzab artza", "sullam" rashe tebot: s'kor, l'yemunim, m'ym; kepi hasseder hazzeh taaseh vekannizkar baacharonim za"l.

clarification.explanation: Regarding a sour lemon, some hold it is forbidden to squeeze it into an empty vessel even if the intent is to place it on food, since in places where lemons are plentiful, people commonly squeeze many of them into a beverage called "lemonade" and fill large barrels with it. Although Maran (the Shulchan Aruch) permitted squeezing it, it appears that in our time the stricter view is correct, and so the later authorities — and also the Chida — ruled not to squeeze a sour lemon into an empty vessel. One who wants to prepare "lemonade" (a lemon drink with sugar and water) must first put sugar in the vessel, and squeeze the lemon onto the sugar itself (which is food), and only afterward add water — but it is forbidden to add water before squeezing the lemon. A mnemonic for this: "SLM" — sugar, lemons, water — in this order it must be done.
takeaways: A sour lemon — in practice should not be squeezed into an empty vessel, even for the purpose of placing it on food.
To prepare lemonade, first put sugar in the vessel, squeeze the lemon onto it, and only then add water — in the order: sugar, lemons, water.

paragraphs: Keshem shehassechita asura beshabbat kak asura beyom tob, v"p shehi letzorek okel nepesh; ella shebbeshabbat asura min hattora, ubeyom tob asura middibre soperim, sheggazeru bazeh shemma yitrach beyom tob laasot harbeh gam letzorek chol, dederek haolam laasot zeh letzorek yamim rabbim, vekannizkar besiman ttzh, yeuyyan sham. vehinneh poh irenu bagdad y" nohagim lischot rimmonim chamutzim vegam et habboser beyom tob letok qeara reqanit, veaach"k notenim et hammayim hannizkarim letabshil lebashshelo bahem kede sheyyihyeh chimmutz, ak qodem shessochatin et habboser veet harimmonim, darkam leshelleqam techilla bemayim al haesh, veaach"k sochatim otam kede sheyyihyu nochin lehissachet yapeh benaqel. venireh li leyashsheb hamminhag shennahagu lischot liqara reqanit velo lehaokel - mippene ki beyom tob hassechita mutteret min hattora mishshum okel-nepesh, vachakamim gazeru leesor shemma yaaseh harbeh letzorek chol; veellu, kevan desholeqim otam techilla, i epshar lischot mehem harbeh letzorek chol, ki yitqalqel hammashqeh hannischat mehem velo yitqayyem ella letzorek bo bayyom davqa, veal-ken bazeh la shayeka gezerat chaza"l.v"g deosim ken gam beboser vekatabti leel (halaka d) deyesh oserin lischot habboser gam letzorek haokel - epshar lomar demodo beboser shaluq, mippene ki bishliqa nechelash qoshi chamitzuto, veyihyeh rauy qetzat laakila, veen lo din boser hannizkar leel; ken nireh li leyashsheb hamminhag.

clarification.explanation: Just as squeezing is forbidden on the Sabbath, so it is forbidden on a Festival as well, even though labors for the sake of food preparation are permitted on a Festival. The difference is that on the Sabbath squeezing is Torah-forbidden, while on a Festival it is forbidden only rabbinically, since the Sages decreed lest one come to exert great effort and prepare also for the weekdays (since it is the world's way to make these beverages in quantities for many days). In Baghdad the custom was to squeeze sour pomegranates and also unripe grapes on a Festival into an empty bowl, and then use the squeezed liquid to cook a dish in order to sour it — but before squeezing, they were accustomed to parboil (cook briefly) the pomegranates and unripe grapes in water over the fire so they would be easier to squeeze. The Ben Ish Chai reconciles this custom: since the fruits are parboiled first, it is impossible to squeeze a large quantity from them for the sake of the weekdays (since the squeezed liquid spoils and does not last beyond that day), and therefore the Sages' decree forbidding squeezing for a Festival does not apply here. Likewise regarding unripe grapes, although it was mentioned above that some forbid squeezing them even into food, it is possible they would agree that unripe grapes that have already been parboiled somewhat are fit for eating and do not have the law of ordinary unripe grapes.
takeaways: Squeezing is forbidden on a Festival too, but only rabbinically (out of concern for preparing for the weekdays), whereas on the Sabbath the prohibition is Torah-level.

The Baghdad custom of parboiling pomegranates and unripe grapes before squeezing on a Festival resolves the concern about preparing for the weekdays, since the squeezed liquid does not last for additional days.

paragraphs: Zetim vaanabim shennitrassequ mibbeod yom, mashqin hayyotzein mehem beshabbat muttarin, dekevan denitrassequ, nimtza hammashqeh zab meelayv vela gazerinan shemma yischat, daapillu im yischatem la abad issur tora ella issur derabbanan mippene shehammashqeh zab meelayv mikkoach harissuq, ella sh"y hassechita memaher latzet. vaapillu im lo nitrassequ, ella im yesh yayin begigit shehaanabim betokah, "p shehaanabim mitbaqqeim beshabbat veyatza mehem yayin, muttar lishtot miggigit zo beshabbat, mippene dekol meat yayin hayyotze min haanabim beshabbat mitbattel beshishshim, kevan shehaya baggigit miqqodem kenisat shabbat; v"p shehu dabar sheyyesh lo mattirin, ki hu muttar achar shabbat belo bittul, mikkol maqom kevan shello haya nikkar qodem shennitareb, velo haya alayv shem yayin meolam, let beh hay dina. umittaam zeh muttar litten hatztzimmuqim letok hammayim meereb shabbat "p shello nitrassequ mibbeod yom, vehem mitbaqqeim beshabbat "y sheriyyatan bemayim veyotze mehem yayin, dekol hayyotze mehem mitbattel qamma qamma bemayim shennasheru bo veshari; ak tzarik lehazhir hamon haam lebilti yischatu hatztzimmuqim beyadayim beshabbat kaasher yiru hammayim muatin, deyesh bazeh chiyyub chattat; veayyen "chayye-adam", kelal y"d, ot y"d. vekol zeh eno ella benoten haanabim mibbeod yom letok hayyayin, abal beshabbat atzmo asur litten anabim betok hayyayin kede sheyyitbaqqeu veyotziu yenam, d"g deeno sechita beyadayim, mikkol maqom sechita kilachar yad asur midderabbanan. veim abar venatan, muttar lishtot min hayyayin, mippene shehammashqin hayyotzein meellu haanabim betelim bishar hayyayin shebbakkeli qamma qamma ukemo shekkatub baacharonim za"l. veda, ha deasur litten tzimmuqim bemayim beshabbat kede laasot mashqeh - millebad issur leta dischita, od ikka issura dekobesh kebashin, dehu leta dimbashshel, ukemo shekkatab harab "shulchan-atze-shittim" za"l.

clarification.explanation: Olives and grapes that were already crushed before the Sabbath — the liquid that emerges from them on the Sabbath is permitted, since, having already been crushed, the liquid drips on its own and there is no concern one will come to squeeze them, and even if one does squeeze — it is only a rabbinic prohibition and not a Torah one, since the liquid was already dripping by force of the crushing and the squeezing only hastens its emergence. Likewise, if there is wine in a vat with the grapes inside it, even though the grapes burst open on the Sabbath and wine emerges from them, it is permitted to drink from the vat, since the small amount of emerging wine is nullified in sixty parts within the wine that was already in the vat before the Sabbath. For the same reason it is permitted to place raisins in water already on the Sabbath eve, even though they burst on the Sabbath and wine emerges from them — since whatever emerges from them is nullified at every moment in the water that had already absorbed it beforehand. But people should be warned not to come to squeeze the raisins by hand on the Sabbath when they see the water is scanty, since this carries a sin-offering liability. This entire leniency applies only when the grapes are placed in the liquid before the Sabbath — but on the Sabbath itself it is forbidden to place grapes into wine so that they burst, since even though this is not actual squeezing by hand, indirect squeezing is rabbinically forbidden. And if one transgressed and did so, after the fact it is permitted to drink the wine, since the liquid that emerged is nullified at every moment in the rest of the wine. One should know that the prohibition of placing raisins in water on the Sabbath is not only due to squeezing, but also carries an additional prohibition of "pickling," which is a derivative of the prohibition of cooking.
takeaways: Fruits crushed before the Sabbath — the liquid that emerges from them on the Sabbath is permitted, since it is not considered squeezing but self-drainage.

On the Sabbath itself it is forbidden to place grapes or raisins into a beverage so that juice emerges, even indirectly — but after the fact, the beverage is permitted to drink under the rule of nullification.

paragraphs: Muttar lischot bepiv hammashqeh min happerot, mippene deen derek sechita bekak; v"g deyesh oserin - haiqqar kisbarat hammattirin; veraq bezetim vaanabim nakon lehachmir bimtzitza. umikkol maqom asur limtzotz dam shebben hashshinnayim veliplot, v"g dehave mepareq kilachar yad, apillu hake asur middibre soperim, veayyen acharonim za"l.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to suck a beverage from fruits with the mouth, since this is not the normal manner of squeezing, and although some disagree, the primary halacha follows the lenient view. But with olives and grapes it is proper to be stringent and not suck them with the mouth. Nevertheless, in any case it is forbidden to suck blood that emerged from between the teeth and spit it out, since although this is an indirect labor, the Sages nonetheless forbade it.
takeaways: It is permitted to suck a beverage from fruits with the mouth (except olives and grapes, where it is proper to be stringent), since this is not the normal manner of squeezing.
It is forbidden to suck and spit out blood from between the teeth, even though this is an indirect labor.

paragraphs: Hashsheleg vehabbarad, asur lerasseqan beyadayim, dehaynu leshabberam lachatikot daqqot kede sheyyazubu memehen; ushene teamim yesh baddabar: chada, gazerinan shemma yischat perot haomedin lemashqin; veod, mishshum serek melaka nageu bah, dedame limlaka shebbore hammayim haellu, vekannizkar b"bet-yosep", siman shy"ch vesha"k, yeuyyan sham. vehannotel yadayv bachorep bemayim sheyyesh bahem sheleg ubarad, yizzaher shello yidchaqem ben shette yadayv, shello yihyeh merasseq beyadayim; mihu, muttar litten chatikot sheleg letok kos shel yayin o mayim bimot hachamma kede letzanneno, vehemma nemochim mealehem veeno choshesh, dekevan deeno oseh beyadayim shari - veyesh mattirin lerasqo beyadayim tok kos shel mayim o shear mashqin, kevan shehu mitareb bemayim en lachush. v"g derabbim ugedolim hemma hammattirim bazeh, mikkol maqom kevan demera"n za"l dato kedaat haoserim lerasseq apillu betok kos hammayim, haki naqetinan.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to crush snow and hail by hand — that is, to break them into fine pieces so that water emerges from them — for two reasons: first, there is concern one might come to squeeze fruits intended for beverages; and second, there is a resemblance here to the labor of creating water, a kind of "trace of labor." One who washes his hands in winter with water containing snow or hail must be careful not to press them between his two hands, so as not to crush them by hand. However, it is permitted to place pieces of snow in a cup of wine or water in the hot season to cool them, and they melt on their own — since he is not doing this by hand and it is therefore permitted. Some permit even crushing snow by hand within a cup of water or another beverage, arguing that since it mixes with the water there is no concern; but since Maran (the Shulchan Aruch) ruled according to the stricter view, forbidding even crushing within a cup of water, this is how one should act in practice.
takeaways: It is forbidden to crush snow or hail by hand to extract water from them, out of concern for squeezing and resemblance to the labor of creating water.
It is permitted to place pieces of snow in a cup of a beverage so they melt on their own, but not to crush them by hand even within the beverage, following Maran's ruling.

paragraphs: Keli sheyyesh bo mayim, venaasa al pene-hammayim qerach, muttar leshabber haqqerach kede littol hammayim mittachtayv; abal im hannahar o habbeer naasa qerach al panayv, yesh oserin leshabber haqqerach mippene shehu mechubbar laqqarqa, ukemo shekkatab hammagen abraham za"l, veken pasequ haggaon rabbenu zalman v"shulchan-atze-shittim" vechesed laalapim ushear acharonim. v"g deharab "eliyya rabba" diqdeq min harab ha"lebush" demuttar - kebar katab al debarayv haggaon "eshel-abraham" deeno mukrach. umah shehokicha harab "tosepet-shabbat" lehattir - ayyen mah shekkatab alayv harab "machatzit-hashsheqel". vahagam deharab "maamar-mareddekay" hiskim lehattir dela kehammagen abraham - kevan dekamma min haacharonim nimsheku achar hammagen abraham leesor - ken iqqar; mihu, hattobelim beshabbat letzorek metzuvveh, yesh lahem lismok al hammattirin, ukemo shekkatab harab tosepet shabbat dikbar nahagu lehattir betobelin letzorek metzuvveh, yeuyyan sham.

clarification.explanation: In a vessel containing water on which ice has formed over the surface, it is permitted to break the ice to take the water beneath it. But if an entire river or well has frozen over its surface, some forbid breaking the ice, since it is attached to the ground (and this is considered like a labor performed on something attached to the earth) — and so several of the great later authorities ruled. Some disagree and hold it is permitted, but the practical ruling follows those who forbid it. Nevertheless, one who must immerse on the Sabbath for a religious obligation (for example, an immersion for a commandment that cannot be postponed) may rely on the lenient opinion and break the ice on the river or well.
takeaways: It is permitted to break ice that has formed over water in a vessel, in order to take the water beneath it.
Ice formed over a river or well attached to the ground — in practice should not be broken, except for an immersion for a commandment that cannot be postponed.

paragraphs: Dores adam sheleg beshabbat veeno choshesh "g denimcheh venames, dedabar sheeno mitkavven hu vela have haka pesiq resha, deepshar shello nimcha. ubimqomot shebbime hachorep kol haaretz melea sheleg - "g devadday namas, deha hamminalim lachim hem - hittiru bazeh mishshum dei epshar lehizzaher. veken hu haddin demuttar lehattil me-raglayim bashsheleg bemaqom shekkol hammeqomot meleim sheleg, dei epshar lehizzaher bazeh, abal baaratzot deen kol haaretz melea sheleg tzarik lehizzaher shello yashtin besheleg.

clarification.explanation: It is permitted to walk on snow on the Sabbath without concern, even though it melts and dissolves underfoot, since this is "an unintended act" — the person does not intend to melt the snow, and it is also not certain it will melt (there is no "inevitable certain result" here). And in places where the entire ground is covered with snow in winter, even though it is clear the snow melts (since the shoes get wet), this was nevertheless permitted, since it is impossible to be careful about this. In the same way, it is permitted to urinate on snow in a place where the entire area is covered with snow, since it is impossible to be careful about this; but in lands where not all the ground is covered with snow, one should be careful not to urinate on snow.
takeaways: It is permitted to walk on snow on the Sabbath even though it melts, since this is "unintended" and not certain to happen — and where the ground is entirely covered with snow, it is permitted even though melting is certain, since it cannot be avoided.
Urinating on snow is permitted only where the entire ground is covered with snow and it cannot be avoided; elsewhere one should be careful.

paragraphs: Lo yeshapshep yadayv bemelach mippene shennimmocha al hayyad venaasa mayim. veyesh bazeh otam shene teamim shekkatab mera"n bebet yosep al hashsheleg deasur lerasqo beyadayim; abal baal hatterumot za"l sabar hattaam - hen bemelach, hen besheleg - hu mishshum nolad, verob happoseqim chalequ alayv bazeh; umera"n za"l shehebi din hammelach hannizkar mibbaal hatterumot, pesiq kevateh velav mittameh, deeno modeh letaam shel nolad, ella hu mitteamim hannizkarim bashsheleg. veayyen mah shekkatab "olat-shabbat", siman sha"k, seip qatan k"ch, veshello bediqduq katab ken, devadday mera"n za"l it leh tere tame, veraq taam shel nolad let leh. veayyen "ketonet-yosep", siman y"b. ukeshem sheasur leshapshep yadayv bemelach, kak asur leshapshep keli bemelach, lepi shehammelach nimcha keshechopep bachazaqa, abal im natan melach bammayim ad shennimmocha meelayv betok hammayim, muttar lehaddicha hakkelim beotam hammayim.

clarification.explanation: One should not rub one's hands with salt, since the salt dissolves on the hand and turns into water — and the same two reasons the Shulchan Aruch gave regarding the prohibition of crushing snow by hand apply here. Some say the reason is because of "creating something new" (a novel entity), but most authorities disagreed with this, and Maran ruled the law but not for this reason, rather for the same reasons stated regarding snow. Just as it is forbidden to rub hands with salt, so it is forbidden to rub a vessel with salt as well, since the salt dissolves when rubbed forcefully. But if one puts salt in water and waits for it to dissolve on its own in the water, it is permitted to rinse vessels in that water.
takeaways: It is forbidden to rub hands or vessels with dry salt, since it dissolves and becomes liquid — like the law of crushing snow.
It is permitted to use salt water in which the salt has already dissolved on its own, for rinsing vessels.

paragraphs: "ygvrty" sheqqorin bearbi "laban", shehu qapuy veyabesh, umannichin alayv mayim umochin oto "y kap - heerakti bedabar zeh bitshubati, bs"d, bsh"q "rab-pealim", vekatabti debazeh lekka otam tere tame shekkatab mera"n za"l bebet yosep gabbe sheleg ubarad deasur lerasqo beyadayim; veshub hebeti dibre mera"n za"l besiman shk"ch, seip k"b, gabbe makka, deen sakkin bechalab mippene shehu nimmocha; vekatab bebet yosep dehu duvmya derissuq sheleg ubarad shennitbaer besiman sha"k. vekatabti debeemet hanak tame desheleg ubarad lekka bechalab, ak mukrach lomar demera"n oser bechalab mishshum hattaam shekkatab rashi"y za"l besheleg ubarad, dedame limlaka shebbore hammayim; v"g debeemet yesh lechalleq, dekan en gupo naaseh mayim, veen kan bore mayim, im kol zeh sebira lehu lemaran deyesh leesor mippene shennireh leene haolam kak, dedame lesheleg ubarad lepi reut enayim; velaken leinyan halaka heeleti: meachar demera"n za"l besiman shk"ch hannizkar asar bechalab, dimdamme leh lesheleg ubarad, veken rama" za"l behaggahat hashshulchan, siman shk"v, gam ken katab leesor; veayyen "ketonet-yosep", siman y"b v"kp-hachayyim", ot q'. laken nireh deasur lerasseq ha"yegurete" sheqqorin bearbi "laban" shehu qapuy veyabesh velimchoto bemayim, kedin sheleg ubarad. mihu, katabti depoh irenu bagdad hamminhag pashut veyadua umepursam lehamchot ha"yegureti" haqqarush bemayim, velaasoto beyadayim "y kap hamyuchad lazeh; vekevan sheyyesh kan minhag yadua bazeh, mukrach lomar shennahagu kisbarat haramba"m za"l udeima, shehem gedolim veken rabbim, disbira lehu: muttar lerasseq hashsheleg vehabbarad letok hammayim, velo aseru ella raq lerasqo beyadayim shello betok hammashqeh; velaken, kevan demannichin mayim betok zeh ha"yegurete" umamchin oto bo - nahagu hetter bekak veen limchot beyadam, veraq hammachmir tabo alayv beraka.

clarification.explanation: "Yogurti" (called "laban"), which is curdled/set and dry, and which people are accustomed to pour water over and mash with a spoon — the Ben Ish Chai discusses this at length in his book "Rav Pe'alim," and writes that the two reasons that forbade crushing snow and hail do not apply here. But he found that Maran forbade in another place (regarding milk melted onto a wound) for a different reason — that it visually resembles crushing snow, even though there is no actual "creation of water" here, since the substance of the milk does not turn into water. Therefore the Ben Ish Chai concluded that regarding "yogurti" as well one should forbid mashing it in water, following the law of snow and hail, based on this resemblance. However, since in Baghdad the simple and well-known custom is nevertheless to mash the curdled "yogurti" in water by hand and with a spoon designated for this, the Ben Ish Chai concludes that the custom is based on the view of the Rambam and his followers, who hold that it is permitted to crush snow and hail into water (and only forbade crushing them not within a beverage) — and therefore one should not protest against those who follow this practice, and only one who wishes to be stringent with himself — blessing will come upon him.
takeaways: Although there is reasoning to forbid mashing curdled "yogurti" in water like the law of snow and hail, the accepted custom in Baghdad permits it, based on the Rambam's view.
One should not protest against those who follow the accepted custom; only one who is stringent with himself is praiseworthy.

paragraphs: Sukkar sheqqorin bearbe "qnd", shehu metuqqan "y ummanim beeroppa, veasuy chatikot gedolot veqashot, muttar lerasqo betok hammayim limchoto bahem. veayyen "chayye-adam", kelal y"d, ot y", shekkatab: sukkar, muttar lerasqo beyadayim, kevan dilolam okel hu, ayyen sham. vbsh"q "rab-pealim" hebeti debarayv ellu upilpalti bahem, vekatabti deyesh chilluq gadol ben soker uben sheleg ubarad; ulepi zeh, apillu lemera"n za"l deasar besheleg lerasqo tok hammayim, yodeh kan deshare. vekatabti: lepi minhag irenu limchot ha"yegureti" hannizkar leel tok hammayim, az gam hamchaat hassoker betok hammayim shari beli piqpuq; vekatabti daapillu hammachmir b"yegoreti", en tzarik lehachmir besukkar.

clarification.explanation: Sugar (refined by craftsmen, in large hard pieces) may be crushed in water to dissolve it. The author of "Chayei Adam" writes that sugar may be crushed by hand since it is always considered food. The Ben Ish Chai, in his book "Rav Pe'alim," explains that there is a great difference between sugar and snow or hail, and therefore even according to Maran, who forbade crushing snow within water, here it should be permitted. And since the practice in Baghdad already permits mashing "yogurti" in water, all the more so it is permitted without any doubt to also mash sugar in water, and even one who is stringent regarding "yogurti" need not be stringent regarding sugar.
takeaways: It is permitted to dissolve hard sugar in water, since sugar is always considered food, unlike snow and hail.
Even one who is stringent regarding "yogurti" need not be stringent regarding dissolving sugar in water.

paragraphs: Borit, sheqqorin bearbe "tzbvn" (sabbon), sheasuy chatikot yebeshot, verochatzin bo "y meat mayim sheshshopekim alayv veal yadayv beyachad, yesh leesor gam poh irenu y"; udelo keharab "pachad-yitzchaq" veginnat veradim shehittir bazeh, shehaiqqar kisbarat harab "yad- aharon" leesor habborit middina. vahagam ki habborit rochatzim bo im mayim, mikkol maqom beet shemmemachehu beyadayv en mayim beayin im habborit, ki im lichlucha uretibut shel hammayim shennishpeku alehem. veken hamminhag pashut poh irenu shello lirchotz bachatikot borit, ella memachin habborit bemayim meereb shabbat ad shennaasa kullo mayim, veaz rochatzin beshabbat beoto hammayim shennimcha bahem habborit meereb shabbat.

clarification.explanation: Soap made in dry pieces, which people wash with by pouring a little water over the hands and the soap together — this should be forbidden even in Baghdad, unlike the view of some authorities who permitted it, but rather following the stricter view in practice. The reason is that while mashing the soap by hand, there is no actual water present with the soap, only moisture from the water poured over them beforehand — and this resembles crushing something dry. Therefore the simple custom in Baghdad is not to wash with dry pieces of soap, but rather to dissolve the soap beforehand (on the eve of the Sabbath) until it becomes entirely liquid, and then to wash on the Sabbath with that water already dissolved from before the Sabbath.
takeaways: It is forbidden to dissolve dry soap on the Sabbath by rubbing it with a little water poured over it.
The soap should be fully dissolved before the Sabbath, and only the pre-prepared liquid used on the Sabbath.

paragraphs: Peri sheqqorin bearbe "meshammesh" shennityabbeshu harbeh, darkam lishrotam bemayim, umeshapshepim otam beyadayim zeh bazeh ad shennimchim legamre veyihyu mayim, velo yishshaaru ella haggarinim bilbad - heeleti bsh"q "mqbtzl" bs"d, delekka bazeh mishshum memacheq, deha katab rama" besiman shk", seip y"t: muttar lachaloq haokel beshabbat, vela have bazeh memacheq, hoil veepshar leakelo belo zeh veku', ayyen sham. vezeh ha"meshammesh" hayyabesh achar shennasheru - epshar leakelo belo zeh; vegam mitztzad shemmamcheh oto beyadayim, bazeh hashshipshup vechikkuk shemmechakkeko en chashash, ukemo shekkatabti leel (halaka yd) gabbe sukkar; amenam mitztzad hashsheriyya - im hem yebeshim harbeh shei epshar leakelam belo sheriyya, yesh lepaqpeq bazeh mimmah shekkatab rama" za"l behaggahat hashshulchan, siman shy"ch, seip d': kol dabar qasheh sheeno rauy leakelo kelal belo sheriyya, asur lishroto beshabbat, dehave gemar melaka, ayyen sham. vekatab b"chayye-adam", kelal k', seip v', daapillu im shoreh oto betzonen, chayyab; veayyen b"nishmat-adam", ot Adonai, veayyen leharab chesed laalapim besiman shl"v, ot t' shekkatab: perot hayyebeshim, yesh oserim lishrotam beshabbat, vetob lishrotam meereb-shabbat, "sh; al-ken tzarik lehazhiram poh irenu shello yasheru mizzeh hammin sheqqorin "meshammesh" im hem yebeshim harbeh, sheen reuyim leekol qodem sheriyya kelal.

clarification.explanation: A very dried-out apricot, which people are accustomed to soak in water and rub by hand until it dissolves completely into a liquid (leaving only the pits) — the Ben Ish Chai writes in his book "Miqabtzeel" that there is no problem of "smoothing" (the prohibition of leveling/mashing into a uniform paste) here, since the Rema wrote that it is permitted to divide food on the Sabbath and this is not considered smoothing, since it can be eaten even without this division. A dried apricot after soaking can be eaten even without the mashing, and also regarding the mashing and rubbing itself — as written above regarding sugar — there is no concern. But regarding the soaking in water itself — if the apricot is so dry that it cannot be eaten at all without soaking, there is room for concern, since the Rema wrote that a hard item entirely unfit for eating without soaking may not be soaked on the Sabbath, since this is considered "completing the manufacture." And even if soaked in cold water, there is liability for this. Therefore one should be warned not to soak a very dry apricot that is entirely unfit for eating before the soaking, even though after soaking it is permitted to rub and mash it. And regarding dried fruits in general — some forbid soaking them on the Sabbath, and it is good to soak them before the Sabbath.
takeaways: Mashing an already-soaked dried apricot by rubbing with the hands is permitted, since it is fit for eating even without the mashing.
But if the apricot is so dry that it is entirely unfit for eating without soaking in water, it may not be soaked on the Sabbath itself — it should be soaked beforehand.

paragraphs: Yesh min mashqeh sheshshotin oto habberiim, veeno biklal mashqin sheshshotin lirpua, deit behu gezerat shechiqat sammanim; vezeh qorin bilshon arbe "gilab" (me chumtzat limon im abqat soda lishtiyya) ubilshon ashkenaz "smtvvtr" (soda); vedarko sheyyabiu melach chamutzin, dehaynu shennaasa min mayim shel "limonim" chamutzin, vehi yabesh usechoq keapar, umannichim immo sukkar, umannichim bo mayim beshabbat, venotenim letoko sam hanniqra bilshon ashkenaz "suda", vekaasher mitarebim zeh im zeh yachad, oseh pipua harbeh, veshotin oto tekep beet happipua. veheeleti bitshuba, bs"d, bsh"q "rab-pealim", demuttar laasot zeh beshabbat lishtoto, veen lachush mishshum mebashshel mippene shemmaaleh reticha bazeh happipua, vegam en lachush mishshum dehave lah molid dabar chadash bazeh happipua vedame limlaka; vehebeti sham dibre haggaon "ameri bina" za"l, bemaptechot hasseper shennidpas sham hashshemitta achat bedine shabbat, sheddibber beinyan zeh beqitztzur, vechash im have zeh kemo makkeh bepattish, denaasa berega echad "y maasayv; veod nistappeq im yesh maqom leesor kemo kobesh kebashim veku', vehinnicha betzarik iyyun yeuyyan sham. vaana abda berarti haddin bekol hane sepeqot, veheeleti bs"d al pi reayot demuttar laasot ken beshabbat.

clarification.explanation: There is a beverage that healthy people drink (not for medicinal purposes, which carries the decree against grinding medicinal ingredients), called in Arabic "gilab" and in Ashkenazi usage "soda" — made from dried, ground sour lemon salt (which looks like dust), mixed with sugar, to which water is added on the Sabbath, and then a powder called "soda" is added, and when they all mix together a strong fizzing occurs, and the beverage is drunk immediately during the fizzing. The Ben Ish Chai writes in his responsum in the book "Rav Pe'alim" that it is permitted to prepare and drink this beverage on the Sabbath — there is no need for concern that this involves the prohibition of "cooking" (despite the rising bubbling from the fizzing), and no need for concern that this involves "creating something new" (a labor-like novel creation). He also brings the hesitation of another authority who was concerned that this resembles "the final hammer blow" (since it happens in an instant) or "pickling," but leaves this as requiring further study. The Ben Ish Chai himself investigated all the doubts and ruled definitively that it is permitted to make this beverage on the Sabbath.
takeaways: It is permitted to prepare and drink on the Sabbath an effervescent beverage made of lemon salt, sugar, water, and soda powder, despite the strong fizzing it produces.
There is no concern here of cooking, creating something new, the final hammer blow, or pickling, as the Ben Ish Chai ruled after thorough investigation.
